findings.description: No server_side_encryption_configuration block is defined, so objects — including the uploaded vendor-roster.xlsx — are stored without an enforced SSE-KMS/SSE-S3 default. Any object PUT without an explicit encryption header lands unencrypted.

The bucket declares no ACL and there is no companion aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block resource, so there is no guardrail preventing a future public ACL or public bucket policy from exposing the report and vendor-roster data.
Versioning is not enabled, so object overwrites and deletions (accidental, malicious, or ransomware-driven) are unrecoverable and leave no prior-version forensic record.
No logging block is configured for a bucket that stores vendor roster data, so object-level access to this data leaves no audit trail in the audit_trail bucket that other buckets use.
This bucket holds ledger/financial exports but defines no server_side_encryption_configuration, leaving stored data unencrypted by default at the bucket level.
No bucket policy denying requests where aws:SecureTransport is false, so financial ledger exports may be read or written over unencrypted HTTP connections.
No aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block accompanies this bucket; the private ACL alone does not prevent a later bucket policy or ACL change from making financial exports publicly readable.
Versioning is disabled on a bucket containing financial ledger exports, so deletion or tampering of exported records cannot be detected or rolled back.
No logging block is configured, so access to financial ledger exports is not recorded to the audit_trail bucket.

Despite versioning and access logging being configured, no server-side encryption default is set, so model artifacts (which frequently embed training data or proprietary parameters) are stored unencrypted.
No aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block resource is associated with this bucket, leaving no account- or bucket-level guardrail against public ACLs or policies.
Operational runbooks commonly contain internal hostnames, escalation procedures, and occasionally embedded credentials, yet this bucket defines no default server-side encryption.
No aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block is configured, so nothing structurally prevents runbook content from being exposed publicly by a future ACL or policy change.

force_destroy = true on the bucket that receives access logs for model_artifacts allows Terraform to delete the bucket and all audit evidence in a single apply, enabling destruction of the forensic trail.

The ACL value 'lcatalogopts-delivery-write' is not a valid canned ACL and appears to be a corrupted 'log-delivery-write'. Relying on legacy ACL grants for the audit log destination is fragile; access control for a log sink should be enforced by an explicit bucket policy restricted to the logging service principal and source bucket.

The audit log destination bucket has no aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block, so access logs — which reveal object keys, requester identities, and access patterns — are not protected against inadvertent public exposure.

A vendor roster spreadsheet is uploaded with neither server_side_encryption nor kms_key_id set, into a bucket (reports_archive) that also has no default encryption rule, so this potentially sensitive third-party data is written to S3 in plaintext.
